paras: The Dublin Republican convention incident was the ordering out of town of two Black delegates from Thurber who had come to Dublin, Erath County, Texas, for a Republican county convention called for August 16, 1890. All accounts agreed that the delegates were told to leave, but they differed on who gave the order, whether the delegates left, and why the convention failed. A report from Thurber calling the affair an outrage drew public denials from a Dublin citizens' meeting and from the town's mayor, and the county convention met at Dublin ten days later.

The Republicans of Erath County had called their county convention to meet at Dublin on Saturday, August 16, 1890. The county executive committee was chaired by G. N. Arnold, a Dublin resident whom a later dispatch identified as the town's postmaster. Thurber, in the same county, sent a party that included two Black delegates.

According to the Dublin citizens' letter, the two Black delegates arrived on the Rio Grande train the night before the convention. Mayor R. H. McCain wrote that as they walked up town from the depot, "one or two irresponsible persons" told them they had better "git" because those persons did not want a Republican convention in Dublin. The citizens' letter put it more directly, saying the delegates were ordered to leave "not on account of their politics, but their color."

McCain stated that the matter was reported to him at once and that he met Arthur Miller and Ed Pierson, two white men who had come with the delegates. By his account, he and Arnold went to the Black delegates, promised them protection, and persuaded them to stay, and also urged Miller and Pierson not to leave. The Thurber correspondent told it differently: the delegates "received their 'orders'" and drove home as fast as their teams could carry them.
On the morning of August 16, McCain wrote, only twelve or fifteen delegates arrived, and Arnold and others decided not to hold the convention for that reason, not out of fear.

On Friday, August 22, a mass meeting of Dublin citizens adopted resolutions deploring "the action of one or two persons" and declaring that it did not reflect local feeling toward people "of any color or political faith." The resolutions called a Stephenville Empire report that Republicans had been driven out a "base slander," denied the Empire's statement that two citizens had been arrested, and promised an investigation. Arnold and other Dublin Republicans endorsed the resolutions in a signed statement.

The Erath County Republican convention met at Dublin on August 26, with R. H. Townsend as temporary chairman, and elected Arnold, E. J. Hewlett of Stephenville and I. G. Monroe of Thurber as delegates to the state convention.

The episode appears only in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, a white daily; no Black-press account was found. The Gazette first printed an unsigned Thurber special on August 26 under the heading "Republican Convention Broken Up," which blamed "the hoodlum element of Dublin" and "darklantern clans" and called the affair an "infamous outrage." That dispatch invited the county's Republicans to meet instead at Stephenville, where they would have "every protection."

Within four days the Gazette gave space to two replies from Dublin, the citizens' letter on August 29 headed "The Report that Republicans were Driven Out of the City Indignantly Denied" and the mayor's letter on August 30 headed "The Full Facts." McCain faulted the Thurber writer for lacking "nerve enough to sign his name," called the episode a "little matter," and said he had kept the white Thurber men from leaving to avoid "a big bloody shirt wave."

The Thurber correspondent described organized "darklantern clans," whereas the Dublin letter, the resolutions and the mayor blamed only "one or two" persons. The accounts also differed on the Thurber party, which the correspondent described as four delegates including "a couple of negroes" and McCain as two Black delegates, one white delegate and a white Democrat who came along. On whether the delegates went home, the only versions are an anonymous Thurber report and the mayor, who wrote to defend Dublin's "good citizens and peace officers."

reader.title: Dublin Republican convention incident
bases: Two Black delegates visiting Dublin for a Republican county convention were told to leave town because of their color (A3, A7); whether they actually left is disputed (A1 vs A7), and no violence is reported.

The Thurber report (A1), the Dublin citizens' letter (A3) and the mayor's letter (A7), written by different parties, agree that the Black delegates were ordered to leave; they disagree on scale, organization and outcome.

accounts.label: Thurber correspondent (anonymous)
accounts.gist: Dublin 'darklantern clans' organized to run out the Black delegates and break up the convention; the Thurber delegates received 'orders', went home, and the convention was broken up.

accounts.label: Dublin citizens' letter and resolutions
accounts.gist: Two colored delegates were ordered to leave by 'irresponsible parties' because of their color, not their politics; the act of 'one or two' did not reflect local sentiment, no arrests were made, and an investigation was under way.

accounts.label: Mayor R. H. McCain
accounts.gist: One or two persons told the Black delegates to 'git'; he and Arnold persuaded them to stay; no white delegate was ordered out; the convention was dropped for poor turnout.

accounts.label: Stephenville Empire (as quoted by Dublin resolutions)
accounts.gist: Republicans were driven out of Dublin, sentiment prevented the convention, and two citizens were arrested.

framing.detail: Thurber special headed 'Republican Convention Broken Up' calls it an 'infamous outrage' by the 'hoodlum element of Dublin' and 'darklanternites'.
Dublin letter headed 'The Report that Republicans were Driven Out of the City Indignantly Denied' concedes the order to leave but blames 'one or two persons'.
Mayor's letter headed 'The Full Facts' admits the delegates were told to 'git' but calls it a 'little matter' and warns of a 'bloody shirt wave'.
